To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the neurocomputational model we used to explain context-dependent cataleptic sensitization in rats, based on the reward-prediction-error hypothesis of dopamine function, was able to account for the context dependency, extinction and renewal of this phenomenon.

context-dependent cataleptic sensitization, extinction training, and context-dependent renewal can be explained by a neurocomputational account based on NoGo learning via D2 receptor antagonization in striatopalliadal neurons.
context-dependent cataleptic sensitization, extinction and renewal can be explained by the reward-prediction-error hypothesis of D2 receptor function.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the neurobiology of the sensitization of drug-induced catalepsy in rodents, and the neurocomputational mechanisms that underlie the context dependency and nonextinguishability of this effect.
the development of a computational model of the neural basis of the context dependency of drug-induced behavioral sensitization.
the neurocomputational underpinnings of the behavioral phenomenon of catalepsy and how it relates to the neurobiology of dopamine and the basal ganglia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the novelty model of dopamine function is not the best explanation for context-dependent cataleptic sensitization.
the novelty hypothesis does not explain context-dependent haloperidol-induced catalepsy.

both the novelty and the reward prediction error hypotheses of dopamine function can account for the context-dependent sensitization of catalepsy induced by repeated administration of haloperidol in rats, but the novelty hypothesis cannot account for the context dependency of the phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the novelty hypothesis is insufficient to account for all of the data.
the reward prediction error account provides a better explanation for the behavioral data than does the novelty account.
the reward prediction error hypothesis is a more parsimonious account of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying catalepsy sensitizations than the novelty hypothesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the context-dependent nature of sensitization can be understood as a form of “NoGo” conditioning that is resistant to extinction.

context dependency and non-extinguishability of sensitization may be a result of latent NoGo representations, which are prevented from being learned or unlearned, respectively, during exposure or extinction.
the neurobiological mechanisms underlying the context dependency of catalepsy are likely more complex than previously assumed.
